doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: The Sands with Red Norvo and the Vegas stars
summary: A year at The Sands opposite Red Norvo, watching Sinatra, Nat Cole and others, Louis Prima and Keely Smith, and Sinatra's shirt maker story.

bands.name: Louis Prima and Keely Smith with Sam Butera and the Witnesses

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: In the summer we would take them on the road with us again. We’d go to Reno, go to Lake Tahoe, then make a swing through San Francisco and go down to L.A. and back to Las Vegas, and this time go into The Sands for a year, opposite the Red Norvo Quintet. And that was wonderful, because here we had a good group, a tight group, and Red had a © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
fantastic group. So we were there for a year and we got to meet everybody who came through The Sands. Now that’s Sinatra, Nat King Cole, Jerry Lewis, on and on and on.
Also we attracted all the musicians from the Strip to hear these two groups. So the place was booming. It was wonderful.

It was kind of like going to school. You know you’d go into the — because they’d let you go in the showroom in the back of the room and watch everybody that was there. And that was the most musical, that was the most musical place because most of the places didn’t have very good music, it was all kind of loud, bashey bands. So the only other thing that was happening was Louie Prima was down at the — what was that The Sahara?
Keely Smith and Sam Butera and the Witnesses. And that was the most musical thing there, until we came along.
Keely was a good singer. She still is.

She was good, yeah, and they had an act that made it for Vegas, you know, with all the deadpan and the takes back and forth and the theatricality of that. But we were just doing music. We were just doing good things. And Red Norvo’s group was wonderful, and of course all the guys in the showroom would always come in, like Frank would come in and Nat Cole would come in, and they’d sit in the back at a table and listen to the groups, because it was something they could enjoy.
Or Sinatra would have all the tables lined up right in front of the bandstand in one big long table, like out to the end. And he would invite all these people in to sit all the way around.
Yeah. Occasionally. And I remember this one night, the place is packed. And he calls the head waiter over and he says, “who’s that guy down at the end?”
Someone was there that he didn’t know.

Tell him his membership is up. And the head waiter went down and talked to the guy and he came back to Frank and he says, “no, he’s all right. That’s Joe DiMaggio’s shirt maker.” And Frank says, “okay.”
That was funny you know, because he was a friend of his so he couldn’t throw his shirt maker out. That’s a true story. © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-
